whatIsSection.title: What is a Nuzlocke?
whatIsSection.intro: A Nuzlocke is a self-imposed hardcore ruleset for Pokémon games: less safety net, more attachment to your team — and every route matters. The rules are voluntary and not built into the games; you choose how strict the run is.
rules: Catch only the first wild Pokémon on each route or area — no second chance if it faints or flees.
If a team Pokémon faints, it is dead (release or permanently boxed).
Nickname every Pokémon you catch — that bond is part of the challenge.
whatIsSection.variants: Play solo, pair up in a Soul Link, add a randomizer, run Hardcore (no boxing), or use dupes/shiny clauses — most players customize. This tracker supports solo and multiplayer runs including Soul Link.

about.title: Six tabs fewer.
about.lede: MyPokePanion grew out of one very concrete annoyance — and became a toolkit that bundles everything you actually need while playing.

story.title: Why this site exists
story.text: Whenever I played a Nuzlocke myself, I had five or six tabs open at all times: a wiki for encounters, one for moves, a type chart, a damage calculator, a route list, a team overview. Every single decision in the run meant jumping between tabs. MyPokePanion is the answer: one place that unites exactly this information — fast, beautiful, in German and English.

gamers.title: Built for players
gamers.text: A full dex with sprite museum and descriptions, region maps with encounter tables and items, a Nuzlocke tracker with soul-link co-op, a team builder with legality checks and Showdown export, a versus lab for matchups, and an item lexicon. All tools I wished for as a player myself.

hobby.title: A hobby project
hobby.text: This site is not a company product but a passion project I keep developing in my free time. New features land regularly — and honestly: the best part is feedback from real players.

feedback.text: Found a bug or have an idea that would make the tool better? That helps me more than anything — tell me.

route1.title: Route 1 – Pokémon & Locations
route1.intro: Route 1 is your first step out of Pallet Town – short, calm and trainer-free. The grass holds just two species, but both matter for your run: Pidgey as an early Flying sweeper, Rattata as a solid Normal attacker. Grab your first catch, pick up the free Potion from the Poké Mart clerk and head on to Viridian City. All rates are from FireRed/LeafGreen – identical in both versions.
route1.encounterSource: Source: PokéAPI (FireRed/LeafGreen) – rates are the summed encounter slots.
route1.potionNote: Gift: free sample from the Viridian City Poké Mart clerk standing on the route.
route1.bestCatchBody: Pidgey (50%, Lv 2–5) evolves through Pidgeotto (Lv 18) into Pidgeot (Lv 36) – one of the strongest early evolution lines in FireRed/LeafGreen. As a Normal/Flying type it is immune to Ground, strong against Bug and Grass teams (Viridian Forest, Erika's gym) and later a reliable carrier for HM02 Fly. Rattata is the backup plan: strong early as Raticate (Lv 20), but without the Flying utility.
route1.nuzlockeTitle: Your first catch of the run
route1.nuzlockeBody: Route 1 is the first encounter route of almost every Kanto run: whatever walks into your grass here is your first catch – the dupes clause applies from this point on. Log it in the tracker right away before you move on to Viridian.
route1.nuzlockeCta: Log it in the Nuzlocke tracker
route1.route22Note: Route 22: a dedicated page is coming – until then, all encounters live in the Kanto map.

qa.q: What Pokémon can you catch on Route 1?
qa.aLead: Just two species: Pidgey and Rattata.
qa.aBody: Both appear in the grass at a 50% rate each – Pidgey at Lv 2–5, Rattata at Lv 2–4. The table is identical in FireRed and LeafGreen, and there are no trainers on Route 1.

qa.q: Is Pidgey worth it on Route 1?
qa.aLead: Yes – Pidgey is one of the best early catches in FRLG.
qa.aBody: The line through Pidgeotto (Lv 18) into Pidgeot (Lv 36) delivers strong early stats and useful Flying coverage against Bug, Grass and Fighting. On top of that, Pidgeot is a natural carrier for HM02 Fly later on. If you prefer something more grounded, Rattata is a solid Normal attacker with an early evolution (Lv 20).
The clerk from the Viridian City Poké Mart stands on the route and hands out a free sample. There are no hidden or purchasable items on Route 1.

qa.q: Do FireRed and LeafGreen differ on Route 1?
qa.aLead: No – there is no version difference on Route 1.
qa.aBody: Pidgey and Rattata have identical rates (50% each) and level ranges in both versions. Version-exclusive Pokémon like Growlithe (FR only) or Staryu (LG only) only matter on later routes.

qa.q: What is the best first catch for a Nuzlocke on Route 1?
qa.aLead: Pidgey – because of its evolution line and Flying utility.
qa.aBody: With a 50% encounter rate you have good odds of seeing it as your first encounter. Pidgeot carries you through the early game and stays useful as a Fly carrier. Rattata/Raticate is the workable alternative with an early power spike (Lv 20).

pikachu.whereIntro: In FireRed/LeafGreen there are exactly two wild locations – both with verified rates from PokéAPI:
pikachu.whereNote: Other games? Find every location per route and version in the

qa.aBody: As a pure Electric type, Pikachu has exactly one weakness (Ground) and three resistances: Electric, Flying and Steel at 0.5× each. There are no immunities — the hidden ability Lightning Rod, which additionally nullifies Electric moves, only exists from Gen 5 onward; it plays no role in FR/LG.

qa.aLead: Via a Thunder Stone into Raichu.
qa.aBody: The line starts with Pichu, which evolves into Pikachu through high friendship. Pikachu + Thunder Stone = Raichu; since Gen 7 this yields Alolan Raichu (Electric/Psychic) in Alola instead. No specific level is required for any of the steps.

qa.aLead: Not before Lv 26 – once Thunderbolt is learned.
qa.aBody: In Gen 3 (FireRed/LeafGreen) Raichu learns no new moves by level-up: use the stone too early and you miss Thunderbolt (Lv 26), Agility (33) and Thunder (41). Recommendation: wait for Thunderbolt, then evolve.

qa.q: Which moves does Pikachu learn by level?
qa.aBody: Thunder Shock (Lv 1), Tail Whip (6), Thunder Wave (8), Quick Attack (11), Double Team (15), Slam (20), Thunderbolt (26), Agility (33), Thunder (41) and Light Screen (50). Thunder Wave + Thunderbolt is the standard backbone for a story run.

qa.q: Is Pikachu good for a Nuzlocke?
qa.aLead: Solid, but no free win – with clear strengths and one hard weakness.
qa.aBody: With 90 Speed Pikachu almost always moves first, and Thunder Wave (Lv 8) paralyzes reliably – worth gold for tough catches and fast opponents. Thunderbolt from Lv 26 hits Water and Flying teams hard. The flip side: 35/40/50 bulk is fragile, and its only weakness, Ground, is dangerously common in Kanto (Diglett, Geodude, Giovanni's team). Rule of thumb: great as paralysis support and the anti-Water answer, but never switch it into Ground.

versus.explainerTitle: Who wins? How the Versus Calc works
versus.explainerBody: The Versus Calc pits two Pokémon against each other in a direct duel – with real damage math instead of gut feeling. For every move on both sides you see the damage range: type effectiveness, STAB and the physical/special split are applied accurately per generation. On top of that, the stat delta and speed check compare base stats – moving first decides many duels. Set both Pokémon above and read the matchup straight off.

qa.aLead: It depends on levels and moves – exactly what the calc computes.
qa.aBody: The facts: Pikachu's Electric moves hit Charizard super effectively (2× via the Flying weakness), but Charizard with base 100 Speed is faster than Pikachu (90) and attacks first. Set both above and compare the damage ranges per move together with the speed check.

qa.q: What is super effective against Water?
qa.aBody: Water Pokémon resist Fire, Water, Ice and Steel (0.5× each). Watch out for dual types: Water/Ground (e.g. Swampert) takes 4× from Grass but is immune to Electric. The exact effectiveness per matchup is shown by the calc right in the damage matrix.

qa.q: How is damage calculated in the Versus Calc?
qa.aLead: Per move, using the official damage formula – accurate per generation.
qa.aBody: The base is level, attack and defense stats and the move's power; on top come STAB (same type = 1.5×) and type effectiveness against all of the target's types. The physical/special split follows the selected generation (by type up to Gen 3, per move from Gen 4). The result is the damage range you see in the matrix.
If both of the target's types share a weakness, the factors multiply: 2× · 2× = 4× (e.g. Grass against Water/Ground). Conversely, a weakness and a resistance can cancel out (2× · 0.5× = 1×).

types.title: Pokémon types: all 18 strengths & weaknesses

types.footnote: All data from the current-generation type chart (Gen 9). Dual types multiply the factors — that's why Swampert (Water/Ground) takes 4× damage from Grass.

flavor.normal: The quiet all-rounder: no 2× hits, but only a single weakness — and huge movepools to make up for it.
flavor.fire: The type of story favorites: Charizard, Entei, Arcanine — great against Steel walls, but watch out for Rock Slide.
flavor.water: The most common type in the dex and a defensive bank: only two weaknesses, plus Surf as a mandatory HM in almost every game.
flavor.electric: Only one weakness (Ground) and Thunderbolt as the all-time classic — Flying and Water teams fear it.
flavor.grass: The anti-Water specialist: Water/Ground walls like Swampert take 4× — in return Grass suffers from seven resistances.
flavor.ice: The glass cannon of types: elite offensively against Dragons and Flying, defensively stuck with four weaknesses and one resistance.
flavor.fighting: The wall-breaker: hits Normal, Steel, Rock, Ice and Dark ×2 — no other type cracks as many defensive banks.
flavor.poison: A niche type for ages, the Fairy hunter since Gen 6: Poison Tail and Sludge Wave hit Fairies ×2.
flavor.ground: The Earthquake type: five 2× targets including Steel and Electric — the best attacking type in the game, Flying types aside.
flavor.flying: Immune to Ground and strong against Fighting — the standard coverage type on physical sweepers.
flavor.psychic: The Gen-1 god got tamed over the generations: Dark is immune, Ghost and Bug hit ×2.
flavor.bug: Fast, nasty, underrated: U-turn makes Bug the momentum type — Fire stays the nightmare (Scizor: 4×).
flavor.rock: Hits four types ×2 including Flying and Fire — defensively a construction site with five weaknesses.
flavor.ghost: Immune to Normal and Fighting, and only Steel and Dark resist it — the coverage type for special attackers.
flavor.dragon: The boss type: almost nothing resists Dragon (only Steel), it only hits Dragons ×2 itself — and Fairy is completely immune.
flavor.dark: The Psychic and Ghost killer: Dark hits both ×2 and is immune to Psychic itself — the counter to Gengar and Alakazam.
flavor.steel: The defensive god with ten resistances and an immunity — modest offensively, but every wall in the game loves wearing it.
flavor.fairy: The dragon tamer since Gen 6: immune to Dragon, hits Fighting, Dark and Dragon ×2 — Azumarill shows how scary that is.

item.qa4lead_trade: These Pokémon evolve when traded while holding {{name}}:
item.qa4lead_trade-replacement: {{name}} triggers trade evolutions without trading — examples:

exp-share.verdictLead: A must-have for every story run.
exp-share.verdict: Your benchwarmers level up without any grinding — perfect for keeping the whole team at gym-leader level. In the older games (including FireRed/LeafGreen) it's a held item; in the newer ones it's automatically active for the whole party. For Nuzlocke runs it's pure gold, because it lets you bring replacements up to speed fast.

lucky-egg.verdictLead: The best farming item in the entire game.
lucky-egg.verdict: 50% more EXP for the holder sounds modest but saves hours of grinding across a run — especially before the Elite Four. The catch: the Lucky Egg is notoriously rare, with wild Chansey holding it at tiny odds. If you've got one, keep it on whatever you're currently leveling.

choice-band.verdictLead: One of the strongest damage boosts around — with handcuffs.
choice-band.verdict: +50% Attack is brutal, but you're locked into a single move until you switch. That makes the Choice Band perfect for physical sweepers with one clear job and for U-turn pivoting. Choice Band vs. Life Orb: the Band boosts harder with no HP cost, the Orb lets you switch moves freely — story: Orb, competitive all-in: Band.

choice-specs.verdictLead: The special-attacking take on the Choice formula.
choice-specs.verdict: +50% Special Attack turns any special attacker into a cannon — a Choice Specs Surf or Thunderbolt genuinely hurts. As with every Choice item: one move until you switch. Ideal on fast special sweepers that spam their strongest move anyway.

choice-scarf.verdict: +50% Speed puts slower star Pokémon ahead of most opponents — suddenly your attacker outspeeds half the metagame. The price is the familiar Choice lock. The Choice Scarf is the best revenge-killer item: switch in, outspeed, remove.

life-orb.verdictLead: The Choice Band's more flexible sibling.
life-orb.verdict: +30% damage on ALL moves at the cost of 10% max HP per attack. You can switch moves at any time — exactly what sets it apart from the Choice Band. Head to head: Choice Band boosts harder and costs no HP, the Life Orb keeps you nimble. For story play and long fights, the Orb is usually the more relaxed pick.

eviolite.verdict: ×1.5 to Defense AND Special Defense as long as the Pokémon can still evolve — suddenly pre-evolutions like Porygon2 or Chansey are bulkier than their final forms. The honest answer to 'Eviolite or just evolve?': most of the time evolving wins — but for the few Eviolite aces, the stone is unmatched.

focus-sash.verdictLead: Guarantees you one turn — no matter what hits.
focus-sash.verdict: At full HP you survive any hit at 1 HP, then the sash is gone. That makes it the standard item for fragile leads: laying hazards once or landing one guaranteed counter is almost always in the cards. Watch out for multi-hit moves, weather chip and entry hazards — they bypass the sash.

leftovers.verdictLead: The default item for every tank.
leftovers.verdict: 1/16 max HP per turn, passively, forever — over a long fight that outheals any berry. Leftovers are why walls like Snorlax or Blastoise are so hard to crack: the longer the fight, the more value. Offensive Pokémon usually want more pressure (Life Orb, Choice Band) — but when in doubt: Leftovers is never wrong.

sitrus-berry.verdictLead: The most honest berry in the game.
sitrus-berry.verdict: One-time 25% max HP back, automatically at half health — no RNG, no conditions. For story play and Nuzlocke runs the Sitrus Berry is often the best pick, saving you a healing turn. Leftovers wins the long game — but the berry heals instantly, exactly when things get critical.

lum-berry.verdict: Automatically cures any status condition — including confusion. A Will-O-Wisp burn or sleep can kill entire sweeps; with a Lum Berry you shrug once and attack anyway. It's standard on setup sweepers (dance moves!) because it secures your setup turn.

everstone.verdictLead: A niche item with two clear jobs.
everstone.verdict: First: the holder never evolves — handy if you want to keep a Pokémon unevolved (cuteness or specific level-up moves). Second: in breeding, the Everstone reliably passes down the holder's Nature in older generations. It does nothing for battle stats — and that's fine, that's not its job.

master-ball.verdict: The Master Ball is a 100% catch rate in ball form — which is exactly why you shouldn't waste it on the first Pidgey. The smart rule: save it for roaming legendaries or a shiny that could knock itself out (Explosion!). In FireRed/LeafGreen there is exactly one — at Silph Co. in Saffron City.

ultra-ball.verdictLead: The best ball money can buy.
ultra-ball.verdict: A 2× catch rate at a fair price makes the Ultra Ball the workhorse for every legendary and every stubborn catch. Only when it fails do specialty balls start to shine: Dusk Balls in caves, Timer Balls in long fights, Net Balls against Water/Bug. For 95% of situations the Ultra Ball is the right call.

sun-stone.verdict: Only a handful of Pokémon need the Sun Stone — the best known is the Sunflora line. Because its targets are so specific, the stone sits unused in many runs: check first whether your Grass Pokémon actually evolves with it before hoarding it.

fire-stone.verdictLead: Evolves some of the most beloved Pokémon ever.
fire-stone.verdict: Vulpix → Ninetales, Growlithe → Arcanine and Eevee → Flareon: the Fire Stone has a stacked lineup. The key tip: check the moveset first — many stone evolutions barely learn level-up moves afterwards. Learn your target move first, then use the stone.

water-stone.verdict: Several strong evolutions hang on the Water Stone — above all Eevee → Vaporeon and Staryu → Starmie, a speed demon for the Elite Four. As with all stones: wait until the level-up moves you want are learned — Starmie & co. learn almost nothing afterwards.

thunder-stone.verdict: Pikachu → Raichu and Eevee → Jolteon are the classics. Raichu trades cuteness for raw Speed — in FireRed/LeafGreen it learns no new level-up moves afterwards, so learn Thunderbolt & co. as Pikachu first, then evolve.

leaf-stone.verdictLead: The fast pass for Grass teams.
leaf-stone.verdict: The Leaf Stone evolves several solid Grass Pokémon — including Gloom → Vileplume and Weepinbell → Victreebel. In most runs it's the quickest route to a finished Grass sweeper. As always: secure the level-up moveset first, then evolve — almost nothing comes after.

moon-stone.verdictLead: The stone with the strongest duo.
moon-stone.verdict: Nidorina → Nidoqueen and Nidorino → Nidoking make the Moon Stone a power item: both final forms with their huge movepools are legitimate run carriers. Clefairy → Clefable and Jigglypuff → Wigglytuff work too. In FireRed/LeafGreen you find Moon Stones early on Mt. Moon — investing early pays off.

linking-cord.verdict: Kadabra, Machoke, Graveler, Haunter — some of the strongest evolutions were chained to trading for decades. The Linking Cord from Legends: Arceus finally solves it solo: use it, evolve, done. If your game has this item, trade evolutions go straight onto your radar.

metal-coat.verdictLead: Two jobs: a Steel move boost and two iconic evolutions.
metal-coat.verdict: +20% damage on Steel moves makes Metal Coat a solid held item for Steel Pokémon. Its real value is in trading, though: Onix becomes Steelix, Scyther becomes Scizor — both massive upgrades. If you own either one, the answer is clear: hold and trade.

dragon-scale.verdict: The Dragon Scale has exactly one job: Seadra holds it during a trade and evolves into Kingdra — before Gen 6 the only Water/Dragon Pokémon and a top pick for many teams. Wild Horsea and Seadra lines sometimes carry one — with a bit of patience you can farm it.

kings-rock.verdictLead: Flinch chance plus two trade evolutions.
kings-rock.verdict: Held, King's Rock gives your moves a 10% flinch chance — nice on fast attackers, but no game changer. More important: Poliwhirl evolves into Politoed and Slowpoke into Slowking when traded holding it. Both are strong, underrated final forms — the rock is worth far more than it looks.

dubious-disc.verdictLead: The final step to the Porygon-Z cannon.
dubious-disc.verdict: The Dubious Disc has exactly one function: Porygon2 holds it during a trade and becomes Porygon-Z — one of the hardest-hitting special attackers ever. No other use, no other candidate. If you have a Porygon2: get the disc, trade, destroy (your opponents).

pkmnNuz.1: Yes. Bulbasaur nearly solos the first two gyms (Rock, Water) and brings Sleep Powder — the best catching tool of the early game. Assessment based on stats, matchups and learnset.
pkmnNuz.2: Yes. Ivysaur keeps Bulbasaur's strengths — bulk, status powder, Grass/Poison coverage — and carries you safely through the midgame.
pkmnNuz.3: Yes. Venusaur is a defensive anchor: high special stats, Leech Seed plus Sleep Powder and few dangerous matchups in Kanto. One of the safest Nuzlocke final stages around.
pkmnNuz.4: With patience. Charmander has a rough start (Pewter and Cerulean are both bad matchups) but becomes one of the strongest sweepers as Charizard. Survive the early game and you're rewarded.
pkmnNuz.5: Situational. Charmeleon sits in the awkward middle: no gym really favors it and the stats can't sweep yet. It gets much better at level 36.
pkmnNuz.6: Yes, with a warning. Charizard sweeps large parts of the game, but the 4× Rock weakness turns every Rock Slide into a death trap. Keep it away from Lorelei.
pkmnNuz.7: Yes. Squirtle beats Brock safely, has solid matchups throughout and grows into a bulky anchor with Surf and Ice Beam coverage.
pkmnNuz.8: Yes. Wartortle is the least flashy but most reliable middle stage of the three starters — good bulk, no rough patch, a stable path to Blastoise.
pkmnNuz.9: Yes. Blastoise pairs bulk with Surf/Ice Beam and has only two weaknesses — a safe pick almost everywhere in Kanto, including the Elite Four.
pkmnNuz.26: Partly. Raichu is fast and hits hard but stays frail and learns no new level-up moves after evolving in FR/LG — it rarely lasts past the midgame.
pkmnNuz.133: Yes, with a plan. You get exactly one Eevee per game — the stone choice is final: Vaporeon (bulk) and Jolteon (speed) are Nuzlocke-worthy, Flareon suffers from its movepool.
pkmnNuz.143: Yes. Snorlax is a Nuzlocke tank: massive HP, Thick Fat against Fire and Ice, only a Fighting weakness. Worth the catch — don't forget the Poké Flute.
pkmnNuz.150: Yes, but late. Mewtwo only appears in Cerulean Cave after the Elite Four — too late for the actual run, afterwards it trivializes everything.
pkmnNuz.151: Not legitimately. Mew was event-only in FR/LG — in a legitimate Nuzlocke it simply isn't available.
pkmnNuz.149: Yes, with effort. Dragonite is strong, but Safari Zone Dratini takes patience and the 4× Ice weakness is fatal against Lorelei. Late, but mighty.
pkmnNuz.130: Yes — one of the best Nuzlocke picks, period. Magikarp is cheap and available everywhere, Gyarados brings Intimidate, top stats and Surf. Just beware Electric (×4).
pkmnNuz.94: Yes, if you can trade. Gengar is a fast special attacker whose Levitate negates Ground — in FR/LG it's immune to three types (Normal, Fighting, Ground). Unreachable without a trade partner.
pkmnNuz.18: Early on, yes. Pidgeot reliably carries the early game but gets outscaled by its movepool later — a classic route 1 bird: useful, but replaceable.
pkmnNuz.20: Briefly yes, long-term no. Raticate scores early with Super Fang and Hyper Fang but quickly falls behind stronger Normal types.
pkmnNuz.24: Only situationally. Arbok is FireRed exclusive; Intimidate is nice but the stats are middling. There are better Poison options.
pkmnNuz.97: Yes. Hypno has high special defense and Psychic is strong in Kanto — a reliable special tank available early on Route 11 (as Drowzee).
pkmnNuz.105: Yes. Marowak delivers Ground coverage against Electric and Poison teams; with the (rare) Thick Club it becomes a monster. Solid, if unspectacular.
pkmnNuz.65: Yes, if you can trade. Alakazam is one of Kanto's best special sweepers — Abra is catchable early and the trade evolution turns it into a monster. Extremely frail.
pkmnNuz.112: Yes, late. Rhydon has huge Attack and Defense but 4× weaknesses to Water and Grass — unplayable against the wrong teams, otherwise a wall with bite.

pkmnTiming.133: In FireRed/LeafGreen only the stone decides: Fire Stone (Flareon), Thunder Stone (Jolteon) or Water Stone (Vaporeon) — use it right away, waiting gains nothing. Espeon and Umbreon are impossible in FR/LG because the games have no day/night cycle.
